planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in partial to full shade; let clumps settle undisturbed for a full season before expecting strong bloom.

directions: This East Asian woodland species takes its name from the fine hairs lining the inside of its tubular flowers, a detail visible on close inspection of the paired, dangling blooms along each arching stem. It forms modest colonies under deciduous canopy through slow rhizome spread, favoring the same cool, leaf-littered humus that suits trilliums and hostas. Site it in dappled to deep shade with consistent moisture and minimal root disturbance, dividing only when clumps become crowded after several years. Its understated green-and-cream flowers are easily overlooked but reward gardeners who grow Solomon's seals as a collected genus.

planting.note: Divide and plant rhizomes in early spring in moist, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; established clumps tolerate brief dry spells once rooted in.

directions: Found across Japan, Korea, and parts of eastern China, this taller woodland Solomon's seal is named for its noticeably long, stout flower stalks, which hold the paired bell-shaped blooms well clear of the arching foliage. Growers who maintain a broad Polygonatum collection value it for extending bloom display above the shorter species typically grown. It prefers the same cool, humus-rich forest-floor conditions as its relatives, with steady moisture and protection from midday sun. Clumps expand gradually by rhizome and are best left undisturbed except for occasional thinning.

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions in spring into well-drained, humus-rich soil at a woodland edge; this species tolerates somewhat drier and brighter conditions than deep-forest Solomon's seals.

directions: Native to the Caucasus, Turkey, and parts of Iran, this Solomon's seal grows along shaded scrub and woodland-margin habitats rather than deep forest, making it more forgiving of brighter partial shade than many Asian relatives. Arching stems carry alternating leaves and small paired, drooping white flowers typical of the genus. It adapts well to average garden soil as long as drainage is reasonable, and spreads slowly into a loose colony over several seasons. Gardeners assembling a broader Polygonatum collection will find it a useful, less commonly offered regional counterpart to the familiar European species.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade; this Himalayan montane species appreciates a cooler summer root zone than lowland Solomon's seals.

directions: Collected from Himalayan forest understory in Nepal, Bhutan, and adjoining parts of China and India, this species carries its narrow leaves in whorls along the stem in the manner of Polygonatum verticillatum, to which it is closely related. In cultivation it wants the cool, consistently moist, richly organic soil of its native montane forests, and resents prolonged summer heat or drought. Slender stems and small whorled flower clusters give it a finer, more delicate look than the larger East Asian species commonly grown. It is best suited to shaded rock garden or woodland plantings in climates with mild summers.
sources: Flora of Bhutan (Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in gritty, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade; treat as a cool-summer alpine-woodland plant rather than a lowland shade perennial.

directions: Growing naturally at high elevation across the Himalaya into southwestern China, this compact Solomon's seal takes its name from flowers that arise in pairs along the leaf axils rather than the larger clusters typical of lowland species. Its shorter stature and finer texture suit shaded rock gardens and woodland-edge plantings better than open beds. Like other high-elevation Polygonatum, it prefers cool roots, steady moisture, and protection from prolonged heat, and resents being allowed to dry out in summer. Established colonies spread gradually by rhizome and are best left undisturbed for several years between divisions.
sources: Flora of Bhutan (Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil in partial to full shade; protect from hard freezes in colder parts of its hardiness range.

directions: Found in forest understory from Yunnan across the Himalayan foothills into northern Indochina, this fairybells is named for the small spur at the base of each perianth segment, a distinguishing feature from the more commonly grown Disporum cantoniense. Clumping, cane-like stems carry pointed leaves and nodding, tubular flowers followed by berries in the manner of its relatives. It wants warm-temperate woodland conditions with rich, evenly moist soil and reliable shade, and is less cold-hardy than the Chinese species already common in cultivation. Where marginal, a thick winter mulch helps protect the rhizomes through cold spells.
sources: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh Flora of Bhutan

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; this southern-range fairybells is best suited to warm-temperate and mild-winter gardens.

directions: Native to forest understory of southern China and the eastern Himalaya, this fairybells carries pure white, pendant flowers that stand out against its relatives' typically purple-brown or yellow tones. Clumping stems arise each spring from a slow-spreading rhizome, carrying glossy ribbed leaves similar in form to Disporum cantoniense. It performs best in warm-temperate climates with rich, consistently moist, shaded woodland soil and is somewhat less hardy than the widely grown Chinese fairybells already established in cultivation. Division in spring is the most reliable way to increase stock, as plants resent being moved once settled.
sources: Flora of Bhutan (Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh)
